## Answer

Let $M=(A_{ij})$ be the cofactor matrix. Since $A$ is symmetric, $M$ is also symmetric, and the adjugate identity gives

$$M=M^T=\operatorname{adj}(A)=|A|A^{-1}.$$

Therefore

$$f(x)=\frac1{|A|}x^TMx=\boxed{x^TA^{-1}x}.$$

If the nonzero eigenvalues of the real symmetric matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, those of $A^{-1}$ are $1/\lambda_1,\ldots,1/\lambda_n$. Taking reciprocals does not change any sign. Hence $A$ and $A^{-1}$ have the same positive and negative inertia indices, so Sylvester's law of inertia shows that the two quadratic forms have the same canonical form.

## Answer

The symmetric matrix of the quadratic form is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&0&1\\0&a&-1\\1&-1&a-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The vector $(1,1,0)^T$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $a$. On the orthogonal complement spanned by $(1,-1,0)^T$ and $(0,0,1)^T$, the characteristic equation reduces to

$$(a-\lambda)(a-1-\lambda)-2=0.$$

Thus all eigenvalues are

$$\boxed{a,\ a-2,\ a+1}.$$

The canonical form $y_1^2+y_2^2$ requires two positive eigenvalues and one zero eigenvalue. Checking the only possible zero values $a=0,2,-1$, only $a=2$ gives $(2,0,3)$. Therefore

$$\boxed{a=2}.$$

## Answer

Set $u=x_1+x_2$ and $v=x_1+x_3$. Since $x_2-x_3=u-v$,

$$f=u^2+v^2-4(u-v)^2=-3u^2+8uv-3v^2.$$

The matrix in $(u,v)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}-3&4\\4&-3\end{pmatrix},$$

whose eigenvalues are $1$ and $-7$. Also, the three original linear forms span only a two-dimensional space, so the third eigenvalue is zero. The inertia is therefore $(1,1,1)$, and the canonical form is

$$\boxed{y_1^2-y_2^2}.$$

Hence the correct choice is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

## Answer

The matrix of the original form is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&a\\0&2&b\\a&b&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Because an orthogonal transformation gives the standard form $2a y_1^2-3b y_2^2$, the eigenvalues are $2a,-3b,0$. Comparing traces and determinants gives

$$2a-3b=\operatorname{tr}A=5,\qquad \det A=4-2a^2-2b^2=0.$$

Solving yields

$$(a,b)=(1,-1)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(\frac7{13},-\frac{17}{13}\right).$$

In both cases $2a>0$ and $-3b>0$, while the third eigenvalue is zero. Hence the normalized canonical form is

$$\boxed{y_1^2+y_2^2}.$$

The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

## Answer

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2,-1,-1$, so $\det A=2$ and $A^*=2A^{-1}$. From $A^*\alpha=\alpha$ we obtain $A\alpha=2\alpha$ for $\alpha=(1,1,-1)^T$. Complete it to the orthonormal eigenbasis

$$q_1=\frac1{\sqrt3}(1,1,-1)^T,\quad q_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0)^T,\quad q_3=\frac1{\sqrt6}(-1,-1,-2)^T.$$

Thus, with $Q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)$,

$$Q^TAQ=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1,-1).$$

Spectral reconstruction gives

$$A=-I+3q_1q_1^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&-1\\1&0&-1\\-1&-1&0\end{pmatrix},$$

so

$$\boxed{f=2x_1x_2-2x_1x_3-2x_2x_3}.$$

To normalize the coefficient $2$, take $x=Pz$ with

$$P=Q\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt2,1,1)=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt6/6&\sqrt2/2&-\sqrt6/6\\\sqrt6/6&-\sqrt2/2&-\sqrt6/6\\-\sqrt6/6&0&-\sqrt6/3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Then

$$P^TAP=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1),$$

and the canonical form is $\boxed{z_1^2-z_2^2-z_3^2}$.

## Answer

For

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&-1\\1&2&1\\-1&1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix},$$

the eigenvalue multisets are respectively $\{3,3,0\}$ and $\{3,1,0\}$. Similar matrices must have the same eigenvalues, so $A$ and $B$ are not similar.

They nevertheless have the same inertia $(2,0,1)$ and are congruent. One explicit solution is

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}(\sqrt3-1)/6&(\sqrt3-3)/6&(1+\sqrt3)/3\\(1+\sqrt3)/6&(3+\sqrt3)/6&(\sqrt3-1)/3\\-2/3&0&1/3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its determinant is $\sqrt3/3\ne0$, and direct multiplication gives

$$\boxed{C^TAC=B}.$$

## Answer

Because $C^TAC$ is symmetric, $B$ must be symmetric; hence $\boxed{b=3}$. Now

$$\det B=-5,\qquad \det A=2a-4.$$

The congruence identity gives $\det B=(\det C)^2\det A$. Since $(\det C)^2>0$, the two determinants have the same sign. Therefore $2a-4<0$. As $a$ is a positive integer, $\boxed{a=1}$.

For these values, one valid matrix is

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2&\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{4}-\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\\0&\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\end{pmatrix}.$$

Indeed, $\det C=\sqrt{10}/2\ne0$, and direct multiplication verifies

$$C^T\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}C=\begin{pmatrix}4&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
